documents.unit: Faculty Senate (hosted on Morris Library research guide)
documents.title: AI: Guidelines for SIUC Faculty
documents.date_or_term: Faculty Senate adopted July 2024; page accessed 2026-10-25
documents.summary: A Morris Library research guide summarises three Faculty Senate action items from July 2024: be transparent about AI costs, include a syllabus statement on AI use, and learn the harms of AI requirements or bans. The guidance is general and leaves AI rules to individual instructors; the guide adds a library author's opinions against complete bans and links to sample syllabus statements.
documents.stance_why: The page says the guidelines "are general by design to allow individual faculty members to chose the tools and policies best suited for their students and courses", so the document sets no stance itself and delegates to instructors.

units.why: The Senate adopted guidelines on AI in teaching and research; this states scope and adoption of an institution-level framework ("adopted a set of guidelines addressing AI usage in teaching and research"). P56 fits a framework statement; P84 (how made) fits less because it gives only the date.
units.anchor: adopted a set of guidelines addressing AI usage in teaching and research in July 2024
units.frag_start: The SIUC Faculty Senate adopted

units.why: "These guidelines are general by design to allow individual faculty members to chose the tools and policies" hands the decision to instructors, so P04.
units.anchor: general by design to allow individual faculty members to chose the tools and policies
units.frag_start: These guidelines are general by design

units.why: The page frames the guidelines as three "major action items"; this summarises their structure and the items are coded individually below. P56 as the framework statement.
units.anchor: There are three major action items in the guidelines
units.frag_start: There are three major action items
units.policy: The guidelines list three action items: be transparent about costs, include a syllabus statement on AI use, and educate yourself on the potential harms of AI requirements or bans.
units.fit_note: Summarises the guidance structure rather than stating a principle.

units.why: "Instructors should proactively investigate the accessibility and costs of AI tools before requiring students" is a duty on instructors about cost and access, so P51.
units.anchor: proactively investigate the accessibility and costs of AI tools before requiring students
units.frag_start: Instructors should proactively investigate

units.why: "Instructors should follow the University IT procurement process before requiring students to utilize an AI tool" is an approval step before deploying a tool. P65 (review and approve tools) fits; P92 is about using approved tools, not procuring them.
units.anchor: follow the University IT procurement process before requiring students to utilize an AI tool
units.frag_start: Instructors should follow the University

units.why: "instructors are encouraged to indicate this in their course descriptions and syllabi and include the monetary cost to students" asks for cost disclosure in syllabi. P51 (cost equity) fits best; P09 fits only partly because it concerns cost, not AI expectations.
units.anchor: instructors are encouraged to indicate this in their course descriptions and syllabi
units.frag_start: To this end, instructors are encouraged
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to indicate in course descriptions and syllabi the monetary cost to students of required AI tools.
units.fit_note: Asks for cost disclosure in syllabi, which P51 does not name explicitly.

units.why: "Instructors are encouraged to include clear guidelines regarding the citation and acknowledgment of AI-generated content" in syllabi is encouragement (not a requirement) to put AI expectations in the syllabus, so P09 with modality should.
units.anchor: include clear guidelines regarding the citation and acknowledgment of AI-generated content
units.frag_start: Instructors are encouraged to include
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to include clear guidelines in their course syllabi regarding the citation and acknowledgment of AI-generated content in academic submissions.
units.fit_note: Encouraged, not required, and about citation and acknowledgment specifically.

units.why: "It is vital that students understand how to use AI tools responsibly and recognize the boundaries of legitimate use from the start of a course" states why the syllabus statement matters at course start. P09 chosen as the purpose of the statement; P66 fits less since it is about explaining rules in class.
units.anchor: students understand how to use AI tools responsibly and recognize the boundaries of legitimate use
units.frag_start: It is vital that students understand
units.frag_end: from the start of a course
units.fit_note: Gives the reason for communicating boundaries at the start rather than requiring a statement.

units.why: "Emphasis should be placed on the importance of originality and honesty in using AI-generated content" asks instructors to stress honesty and integrity policies. P95 (honesty as grounds for AI rules) chosen over P29.
units.anchor: importance of originality and honesty in using AI-generated content
units.frag_start: Emphasis should be placed on
units.fit_note: An instruction to instructors to emphasise honesty, not only a reason for AI limits.

units.why: The guide offers "examples of syllabus statements about AI usage"; a support resource for instructors writing policy, so P63.
units.anchor: examples of syllabus statements about AI usage in university courses
units.frag_start: Below are some examples of syllabus

units.why: The guide links a Copyleaks guide on "AI text and plagiarism detection software offered within D2L" and its false flags. P40 (detection tools used) fits only partly because the page describes the tool and caveats, not a rule.
units.anchor: AI text and plagiarism detection software offered within D2L
units.frag_start: From the vendor of the AI text and plagiarism
units.policy: The university offers Copyleaks AI text and plagiarism detection software within D2L; the guide notes it flags text edited with Grammarly or copied from Google Translate.
units.fit_note: Describes the tool and its false-flag caveat; no rule on how it is used.

units.why: "Complete bans of AI in courses run the risk of making work unacceptably difficult for conscientious students or encouraging them to dissemble" argues bans are counterproductive (P82). It is the library author's "professor's opinion", not Senate text.
units.anchor: Complete bans of AI in courses run the risk of making work unacceptably difficult
units.frag_start: Complete bans of AI in courses

units.why: "AI is becoming an integral part of the software tools necessary for research" with examples such as Grammarly, translators and Copilot in operating systems argues AI is embedded everywhere so bans are impractical (P82); it also touches P07.
units.anchor: AI is becoming an integral part of the software tools necessary for research
units.frag_start: AI is becoming an integral part
units.policy: AI is becoming an integral part of the software tools necessary for research, including search engines, voice assistants, speech tools, writing software, translators and operating systems.
units.fit_note: Also lists AI built into everyday tools, which P07 would cover.

units.why: "it may be wise to carve out limited exceptions or limit a ban to AI-generated text or images" advises that any ban keep exceptions for routine AI features, so P100.
units.anchor: carve out limited exceptions or limit a ban to AI-generated text or images
units.frag_start: A complete ban disallows all of these uses

units.why: "Educate Yourself on the Potential Harms of AI Requirements or Bans" asks instructors to learn before requiring or banning AI. P102 (stay informed) fits; P63 is institutional support, not a duty to self-educate.
units.anchor: Educate Yourself on the Potential Harms of AI Requirements or Bans
units.frag_start: Educate Yourself on the Potential Harms
units.policy: Instructors are advised to educate themselves on the potential harms of AI requirements or bans.
units.fit_note: Asks for learning about harms of requirements or bans specifically.

units.why: "The Faculty Senate advocates for a culture where ethical considerations such as transparency, accountability, discrimination, bias, and safety are at the forefront" names ethical concerns about AI, so P53.
units.anchor: ethical considerations such as transparency, accountability, discrimination, bias, and safety are at the forefront
units.frag_start: The Faculty Senate advocates for a culture
units.frag_end: of AI use in academic settings

units.why: "We should commit as an institution to ensuring that all AI technologies are accessible to every member of our community, including those with disabilities" is an accessibility commitment, P97.
units.anchor: ensuring that all AI technologies are accessible to every member of our community
units.frag_start: We should commit as an institution
units.frag_end: necessary accommodations to support their use
units.policy: The institution should commit to ensuring all AI technologies are accessible to every member of the community, including those with disabilities, by adopting AI tools that comply with accessibility standards and providing necessary accommodations.

units.why: "All AI models have biases built in. Know what these are before requiring use of a tool." warns instructors about bias before requiring tools, P53. It is the library author's opinion.
units.anchor: All AI models have biases built in. Know what these are before requiring use
units.frag_start: All AI models have biases built in
units.frag_end: before requiring use of a tool

units.why: "Discuss the known issues and any your class discovers with your students" asks instructors to talk with students about AI problems, so P66 (explain and discuss).
units.anchor: Discuss the known issues and any your class discovers with your students
units.frag_start: Discuss the known issues and any

units.why: "Be sure to warn students about submitting personal information, even if the AI tool promises to safeguard inputs" is a privacy duty on instructors, so P50.
units.anchor: warn students about submitting personal information
units.frag_start: Be sure to warn students about
units.fit_note: Directs instructors to warn students; P50 is phrased as protecting data.

units.why: The question of whether a tool's data "automatically go[es] into the training data pool" is a data-privacy caution to check before requiring a tool, P50.
units.anchor: Does it automatically go into the training data pool
units.frag_start: Pay special attention to what a tool

units.why: "An absolute ban cuts off students from technologies which may help them succeed in your course, especially students requiring learning accommodations" argues against absolute bans on access grounds. P51 (accommodations) over P82 because the point is access, not enforceability.
units.anchor: An absolute ban cuts off students from technologies which may help them succeed
units.frag_start: An absolute ban cuts off students

units.why: "Create a general exception for assistive technologies or include a statement that specific exceptions will be made for students requiring accommodations" tells instructors to exempt assistive AI from bans. P97 chosen over P100 because the exemption is for disability access.
units.anchor: Create a general exception for assistive technologies
units.frag_start: Create a general exception for assistive technologies

units.why: The page links a reading list on "academic integrity, environmental impacts, ethics, and legal and privacy issues", pointing instructors to more on harms, so P53.
units.anchor: academic integrity, environmental impacts, ethics, and legal and privacy issues
units.frag_start: Reading list on the various issues

notes: Source is a library-hosted summary of the Faculty Senate guidelines, not the original. Passages labelled "This professor's opinion" are the library author's, coded as guidance on the page but not Senate policy.
